The Many-spotted hummingbird (Taphrospilus hypostictus) is a relatively small-bodied member of the Trochilidae, with adult females reaching an ultimate wet weight of 6.5 grams [Wwi = 6.5 grams] and males attaining a slightly larger body mass of 7.4 grams [Wwi = 7.4 grams]. This modest sexual dimorphism in mass, with males being approximately fourteen percent heavier than females, is less pronounced than in many other hummingbird species where territorial competition often drives extreme size differences. Field workers have noted that the species' slender, slightly decurved bill and predominantly green plumage with distinctive white spotting on the underparts are reliable field marks. The species inhabits subtropical and montane forest edges along the eastern slopes of the Andes, from central Ecuador through Peru to Bolivia, where it forages primarily on nectar from epiphytic and understory flowers, supplementing its diet with small arthropods. Its relatively low wing loading and high metabolic demands, characteristic of the family, necessitate frequent feeding throughout the day.

Respiratory measurements taken during controlled laboratory conditions at a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] have documented a maximum basal metabolic rate of 23.64 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 23.64 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value consistent with the elevated metabolic performance typical of hovering foragers in the family. This rate, nearly an order of magnitude higher than predicted for a non-passerine bird of equivalent body mass under standard allometric equations, reflects the extreme energetic cost of sustained hovering flight, the primary mode of nectar extraction in this species. The metabolic scopes recorded during hovering bouts suggest that the birds operate near their physiological ceiling for extended periods. Environmental temperature fluctuations in the montane habitat likely impose additional thermoregulatory costs, particularly during cooler morning periods when the birds must rapidly elevate their metabolic rate to achieve flight temperatures. Comparative data from related genera indicate that this metabolic profile is finely tuned to the species' altitudinal distribution and nectar resource availability.

Developmental studies conducted at an incubation temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C] reveal that the age at hatching, or the age at birth, is approximately 14.5 days [ab = approximately 14.5 days], a period typical of small-bodied hummingbirds. Neonates emerge from the calcareous egg at a weight at birth of only 0.88 grams [Wwb = 0.88 grams], a strikingly small mass that represents slightly more than ten percent of the ultimate female body mass, underscoring the altricial condition of this species. During the first week of life, the nestlings are brooded almost continuously by the female, who makes frequent foraging trips to provision the rapidly growing chicks. The developmental trajectory is heavily influenced by ambient temperature, with cooler conditions extending the nestling period and increasing the energetic demand on the provisioning parent. The initial mass at hatching places the chicks in a precarious energetic position, as they must quickly double their body weight within the first few days to survive stochastic weather events common in the Andean foothills.

Under the thermal regime representative of the species' active metabolic periods, maintained at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], a predictable developmental schedule emerges. The fledging period, defined as the time since birth at fledging, is completed at 21 days [tx = 21 days], at which point the young bird achieves its first flight and departs the nest at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. Such a small hatchling thus transitions rapidly to a volant juvenile, reflecting a high growth rate fueled by protein-rich arthropod prey delivered by the female. Sexual maturation follows a longer trajectory: the time since birth at puberty is reached at 63 days [tp = 63 days], a developmental milestone that allows the immature bird to attain nearly full adult body mass and exhibit the full plumage characteristics of the species before initiating gonadal development at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. Reproductive maturity, or the time since birth at first brood, is deferred considerably beyond that point, with first successful nesting occurring at 365 days [tR = 365 days], coinciding with the onset of the primary breeding season following the bird's first full year at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C].

The species' maximum documented lifespan, recorded under the standard thermal conditions of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], extends to approximately 2,920 days [am = approximately 2,920 days], equating to roughly eight years for the oldest individuals. This longevity is notable for a bird of such small body size, exceeding the typical three-to-five-year maximum lifespans reported for many temperate-zone passerines of similar mass. Field records of banded individuals suggest that annual survival is relatively high for adult birds, although first-year mortality is substantial due to predation pressure and the challenges of establishing a feeding territory. The species' reproductive output is constrained by a modest maximum reproductive rate: females produce two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch] and typically raise a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], a slow life-history pace that, when combined with extended adult survival, yields a stable population dynamic well suited to the relatively predictable, if seasonal, nectar resources of the montane forest understory.
